q365: The STM32F103C8T6 is a 32-bit microcontroller made by STMicroelectronics that sits on the cheap Blue Pill board; its clock is 72 MHz (four to five times an Arduino Uno), it has 20 KB of RAM and runs on 3.3 volts. Because it's fast and cheap, it's widely used in robots, motor control and more serious projects. We configure it with CubeMX and program it with HAL.
q366: STM32 — setting up pins and the clock in CubeMX
q367: STM32 step one — pin PC13 and the 72 MHz clock
q368: “Unlike an Arduino, an STM32 board leaves everything to you from the very first moment: what each pin does and how many megahertz the chip's clock runs at. The CubeMX tool shows these settings on one graphical page and writes the startup code itself.”
q369:
The Blue Pill has an STM32F103C8T6 chip: a 32-bit Cortex-M3 core up to 72 MHz. In CubeMX you have two main jobs: 1) choose a function for each pin (for example GPIO_Output for the LED on PC13). 2) build the clock: an 8 MHz crystal times a PLL multiplier of 9 gives 72 MHz.

The SWD pins (PA13 and PA14) for the ST-Link programmer and the crystal pins (PD0 and PD1) are set up by CubeMX itself; you don't need to touch them.
q370: The “Clock” tab is open first: press the “Standard 72 MHz” button (or set the PLL multiplier to 9) so that SYSCLK becomes 72 MHz.
q371: APB1 must be divided by 2; this bus's limit is 36 MHz and above that it turns red (the standard button sets this itself).
q372: Then go to the “Cube” tab; the golden box at the top of the page tells you step by step which pin to click.
q373: Click the `PC13` pin (gold) and press `GPIO_Output` from the buttons below; this is the LED on the board.
q374: When the clock has no errors and PC13 is set correctly, the mission completes automatically.
q375: STM32 — connecting the board to the ST-Link
q376: SWD wiring, Connect and uploading the program
q377: “An Arduino Uno comes from the factory with a bootloader and a USB-to-serial converter, which is why it takes a program over a single cable. The Blue Pill has neither; its chip is raw. To load a program you need a separate programmer, and the cheapest and best one is the ST-Link: with two signal wires (SWDIO and SWCLK) it connects directly to the chip's debug section.”
q378:
So far you've only run the program in the simulator. For your code to land on a real board you have to get it from the computer to the chip, and that's the ST-Link's job.

Why a separate programmer? Because the Blue Pill has no USB bootloader, and the F103 chip's ROM has only a serial bootloader (USART1). The micro-USB port on the board can't load a program on its own. The ST-Link writes the flash memory over SWD and also gives you debugging: you can pause the program mid-run and see the values of variables. The Run button in CubeIDE works this same way.

In the simulator below you connect four wires as in real life: 3.3V, GND, SWDIO and SWCLK. Don't connect 5 volts to the board's 3.3 volts, and if you leave one of the wires out or swap SWDIO and SWCLK, the ST-Link gives the same errors as in reality.
q379: First read the “Why a separate programmer?” section; then, with the USB unplugged, start wiring.
q380: Tap one pin on the ST-Link (for example SWDIO) and then its same-named pin on the board; do the same for 3.3V, GND and SWCLK. Read the text next to each pin; the order of the pins on the ST-Link and on the board isn't the same.
q381: Plug the ST-Link into the computer's USB; its LED and the red PWR LED on the board should light.
q382: Press Connect; the ST-Link reads the chip's ID (Device ID 0x410).
q383: Press Upload (Run) to write the blink program to flash. If the LED doesn't blink, check the BOOT0 jumper: it must be on 0, and then press RESET.
q384: When the LED on PC13 blinks, the mission completes automatically.
q387: “On the Blue Pill the PC13 light is wired inverted: when the pin is zero the LED turns on and when it's one it turns off. The HAL_GPIO_TogglePin function flips the pin's state and HAL_Delay waits in milliseconds; these two are the equivalents of Arduino's digitalWrite and delay.”
q388:
You write your own code between USER CODE BEGIN and USER CODE END inside the while(1) of the main.c file; outside these sections, CubeMX wipes everything when it regenerates code.

In the simulator below you do the same: write code that blinks the LED on PC13.
q389: In `while(1)` flip the LED's state with `HAL_GPIO_TogglePin(GPIOC, GPIO_PIN_13);`.
q390: Then write `HAL_Delay(500);` so it waits half a second.
q391: If you like, do the same with `HAL_GPIO_WritePin`: `GPIO_PIN_RESET` turns it on and `GPIO_PIN_SET` turns it off.
q392: STM32 — clock and timer: the chip's heartbeat
q393: The 72 MHz clock, multipliers and building PWM with a timer
q394: “A chip doesn't work without a heartbeat: an 8 MHz crystal ticks, the PLL multiplies it by 9, and the chip takes a step 72 million times a second. A timer is a hardware counter that rides on this same heartbeat and creates counting and PWM without involving the CPU.”
q395:
A microcontroller is a small brain, but it doesn't work without a heartbeat. This beat is the clock; just like a heartbeat, with every tick it pushes the chip one step forward. The faster this beat, the faster the processing. That's why the Blue Pill starts out with an 8 MHz crystal and, with the help of a multiplier (PLL), brings it to 72 MHz; that is, 72 million ticks every second!

But the beat alone isn't enough; you also have to count time. If you use the delay function for waiting, the CPU is like someone staring at a clock and doing nothing else. This is where the timer steps in and hands counting over to hardware: an independent counter that counts ticks behind the scenes and leaves the CPU completely free to get on with its other work.

Once you have a timer in hand, you can switch a pin on and off at high speed; that's PWM. A motor connected to it doesn't feel the rapid blinking and only sees the “average”: on half the time means half the speed!

q415: This is the board's SWCLK, the SWD clock input (the chip's PA14 pin). 👉 Connect it with a wire to the ST-Link's SWCLK (pin 2).
q416: This is the board's SWDIO, the SWD data pin (the chip's PA13 pin). 👉 Connect it with a wire to the ST-Link's SWDIO (pin 4).
q417: This is the board's 3.3V pin and the board draws its power from here. 👉 Connect it with a wire to the ST-Link's 3.3V (pin 7 or 8), not to 5 volts!
q418: Goal: connect the Blue Pill board to the ST-Link with four wires, plug the ST-Link into the computer, Connect to the chip and upload the blink program. Drag a wire from one pin and drop it on its same-named pin on the other side (or tap one pin first and then its same-named pin); tapping a pin that has a wire removes the wire. The four glowing pins of the socket (2, 4, 6 and 8) are the ones you need; the rest are dim and not needed (pins 5 and 7 are equivalent to 6 and 8).
q419: Why does the Blue Pill need a separate programmer?
q420: An Arduino Uno has two things for receiving a program that are fitted to its board at the factory: a “bootloader” inside the chip (a small program that waits for new code) and a USB-to-serial converter chip. That's why a USB cable alone is enough. The Blue Pill has neither.
q422: Built into the chip from the factory
q423: None; it only has ST's own ROM bootloader, which listens only on pins PA9 and PA10 (USART1)
q426: None; the micro-USB port alone can't load a program (the F103 chip's ROM has no USB bootloader)
q428: Available with the ST-Link and SWD
q429: So it becomes a chicken-and-egg problem: to load even a USB bootloader onto the Blue Pill you first need a programmer. The ST-Link connects over SWD, that is, with just two signal wires (SWDIO and SWCLK), directly to the chip's debug section; with it you can write the flash memory, pause the program line by line and see the values of variables. The Run button in CubeIDE does this same thing. Even if a faulty program has locked the chip, the ST-Link can erase it again.
q430: There's a cheaper way too: a USB-to-serial adapter on PA9 and PA10 with the BOOT0 jumper on 1. But it only loads programs (no debugging) and you have to move the jumper every time. The ST-Link is easier.
q432: Always wire first and then plug in the USB. Never give 5 volts to the board's 3.3 V pin; the chip's voltage tolerance is about 4 volts.
q433: GND must definitely be connected, otherwise the ST-Link hears nothing.
q434: The wires connect to the pins inside the ST-Link's black socket; each socket pin lines up with the number and printed name on the body (odd pins 1 to 9 in the left column and even 2 to 10 in the right column). The two GND pins are the same and the two 3.3V pins are the same too; it makes no difference which one you use. SWIM and RST aren't needed for this. The pin order is different on other ST-Links; always read the printed name, not the pin position.
q435: In CubeMX, System Core › SYS › Debug must be set to Serial Wire (the same PA13 and PA14 that were automatically green). If you set No Debug, after the first upload the ST-Link can no longer connect to the chip.
q436: Both BOOT0 and BOOT1 jumpers must be on 0 so the chip runs your program from flash.
